items.topic: regression-t4 · coefficient of determination and adjusted R-squared
items.stem: Consider the simple linear regression model Yᵢ=α+βXᵢ+εᵢ fitted by ordinary least squares using n=10 independent observations. The fitted line is Ŷᵢ=1.5+0.8Xᵢ. Suppose ∑(Yᵢ−Ȳ)²=5 and ∑(Xᵢ−X̄)²=6. What is the adjusted coefficient of determination, rounded to two decimal places?
items.explanation:
We are given n=10, the fitted slope b=0.8, the total sum of squares SST=∑(Yᵢ−Ȳ)²=5, and Sxx=∑(Xᵢ−X̄)²=6.

Step 1: Calculate the regression sum of squares. In simple linear regression with an intercept, SSR=b²Sxx. Therefore SSR=(0.8)²×6=0.64×6=3.84.

Step 2: Calculate the residual sum of squares. The total variation is split into explained and unexplained parts: SST=SSR+SSE. Hence SSE=5−3.84=1.16.

Step 3: Calculate adjusted R-squared. With one predictor and an intercept, the residual degrees of freedom are n−2=8, while the total degrees of freedom are n−1=9. Thus adjusted R²=1−[SSE/(n−2)]/[SST/(n−1)]. Substituting gives 1−(1.16/8)/(5/9)=1−0.130? divided by 0.5556 = 1−0.261=0.739 approximately.

Rounded to two decimal places, adjusted R²=0.74, option A. Do not confuse ordinary R²=SSR/SST=3.84/5=0.768 with adjusted R²; the adjustment penalises the model for estimating a slope parameter. Other-exam relevance: regression sums of squares, R-squared and adjusted R-squared are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · relationship between the two simple-regression slopes
items.stem: For a bivariate data set, one analyst fits Y on X and another fits X on Y, both by ordinary least squares with an intercept. Which pair (slope of Y on X, slope of X on Y) is possible?
items.explanation: The two regression slopes are b(Y on X)=r·sY/sX and b(X on Y)=r·sX/sY. Multiplying them cancels the standard deviations and gives r². Therefore the slopes must have the same sign, and their product must lie between 0 and 1. Option D has two negative slopes and product (−2)(−0.4)=0.8, which is possible. The other options either have opposite signs or a product greater than 1. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · OLS normal equations without an intercept
items.stem: Consider the multiple regression model Yᵢ=β₁Xᵢ₁+⋯+βₚXᵢₚ+εᵢ, with no intercept. Let êᵢ be the ordinary least-squares residual. Which statements are always true?
statements: Σᵢ êᵢ=0 and ΣᵢXᵢ₁êᵢ=0.
ΣᵢXᵢⱼêᵢ=0 for every regressor j.
Σᵢêᵢ=0 and ΣᵢXᵢⱼêᵢ=0 for every regressor j.
ΣᵢYᵢêᵢ=0.

A.why: The model has no intercept, so the sum of residuals need not be zero.

B.why: The OLS normal equations make the residual vector orthogonal to every column of the design matrix.

C.why: It adds the unsupported claim that residuals must sum to zero.

D.why: Y′ê=ê′ê, which is generally positive unless all residuals are zero.

items.explanation: OLS chooses the coefficients to minimise the sum of squared residuals. Differentiating that sum with respect to each coefficient gives the normal equations X′ê=0. In ordinary notation, this means ΣᵢXᵢⱼêᵢ=0 for every regressor j. A zero sum of residuals follows only when the model contains an intercept, represented by a column of ones. This model has no intercept, so statement 1 and statement 3 are not always true. Also, Y=Xβ̂+ê, hence Y′ê=β̂′X′ê+ê′ê=ê′ê, not generally zero. Only statement 2 is always true. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · effect of changing measurement units on OLS
items.stem: In a simple linear regression Yᵢ=α+βXᵢ+εᵢ, both X and Y are converted from square feet to square metres by multiplying every observation by the same conversion constant c. What happens to the fitted intercept and slope?
options: The intercept may change, but the slope will not change
The slope may change, but the intercept will not change
Both the intercept and slope may change
Neither the intercept nor the slope will change
items.explanation: Let Xᵢ*=cXᵢ and Yᵢ*=cYᵢ. The OLS slope is Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)(Yᵢ−Ȳ)/Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². After conversion, the numerator and denominator are both multiplied by c², so their ratio β̂ is unchanged. The intercept is α̂=Ȳ−β̂X̄; after conversion it becomes cȲ−β̂(cX̄)=cα̂. So the intercept changes with the measurement scale, while the slope remains the same when both variables use the same conversion factor. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations. Source-key audit: the supplied answer-key sheet lists A and D for Q34, but D says neither coefficient changes and is contradicted by the intercept formula α̂*=cα̂. Only option A is mathematically correct for a common nonzero conversion factor c applied to both X and Y. The bank therefore retains A and documents the discrepancy rather than copying the inconsistent key.

items.topic: regression-t2 · least-squares estimation, normal-theory MLE and BLUE
items.stem: Consider the model Yᵢ=α+βxᵢ+εᵢ, i=1,2,3, where xᵢ are fixed and the errors are independent N(0,σ²), with α, β and σ² unknown. The observations are (xᵢ,yᵢ)=(1,2.1),(2,3.9),(3,6). Which statements are true?
statements: The maximum-likelihood estimate of α is 0.1.
The least-squares estimate of α is 0.1.
The best linear unbiased estimate of α is 0.1.
The maximum-likelihood estimate of β/α is 19.5.

A.why: The fitted intercept is 0.1, so the MLE and least-squares estimate agree.

B.why: For this normal linear model, least squares minimises the residual sum of squares and gives the intercept 0.1.

C.why: Under the stated independent equal-variance error model, the least-squares estimator is BLUE by the Gauss–Markov theorem.

D.why: The estimated slope is 1.95 and the estimated intercept is 0.1, so their ratio is 19.5.

items.explanation: First calculate the sample means: x̄=(1+2+3)/3=2 and ȳ=(2.1+3.9+6)/3=4. The least-squares slope is β̂=Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ)/Σ(xᵢ−x̄)². The numerator is (−1)(−1.9)+0(−0.1)+1(2)=3.9, and the denominator is 1+0+1=2. Thus β̂=3.9/2=1.95. The intercept is α̂=ȳ−β̂x̄=4−1.95(2)=0.1. In a normal linear regression model, maximising the likelihood over α and β gives the same estimates as least squares, so statements 1 and 2 are true. Because the errors are independent with common variance, the Gauss–Markov theorem says the least-squares estimator is BLUE, so statement 3 is true. Finally β̂/α̂=1.95/0.1=19.5, so statement 4 is true. Therefore all four statements are correct. Other-exam relevance: normal linear regression, least squares, MLE and BLUE are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · unbiasedness and variance comparison of through-origin and intercept OLS slopes
items.stem: Consider Yᵢ=βXᵢ+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, where εᵢ are i.i.d. N(0,σ²) and the nonrandom regressors Xᵢ are positive and distinct. Define β̂₁=∑(Yᵢ−Ȳ)(Xᵢ−X̄)/∑(Xᵢ−X̄)² and β̂₂=∑YᵢXᵢ/∑Xᵢ². Which statements are correct?
statements: Both β̂₁ and β̂₂ are unbiased estimators of β.
β̂₁ has larger variance than β̂₂.
β̂₂ has larger variance than β̂₁.
β̂₁ has the same variance as β̂₂.

A.why: Both estimators are unbiased because each is β plus a linear combination of zero-mean errors.

B.why: Var(β̂₁)=σ²/Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)² and Var(β̂₂)=σ²/ΣXᵢ². Since ΣXᵢ²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²+nX̄² and X̄>0, β̂₁ has the larger variance.

C.why: This reverses the variance ordering; β̂₂ has the smaller variance.

D.why: The variances are unequal because nX̄²>0.

items.explanation: For β̂₁, substitute Yᵢ=βXᵢ+εᵢ. The deterministic part gives β and the error part has expectation zero, so E(β̂₁)=β. Similarly, β̂₂=β+∑Xᵢεᵢ/∑Xᵢ², so E(β̂₂)=β. Thus statement 1 is true. Since the errors are independent with variance σ², Var(β̂₁)=σ²/∑(Xᵢ−X̄)² and Var(β̂₂)=σ²/∑Xᵢ². Now ∑Xᵢ²=∑(Xᵢ−X̄)²+nX̄². Every Xᵢ is positive, so X̄>0 and the denominator for β̂₂ is strictly larger. Therefore Var(β̂₂)<Var(β̂₁), making statement 2 true. Statements 3 and 4 are false. Other-exam relevance: unbiased linear estimation and variance comparison in regression are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi; This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: regression-t7 · heteroscedasticity and weighted least squares / BLUE
items.stem: Consider the simple linear regression model Yᵢ=βxᵢ+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, where E(εᵢ)=0, Cov(εᵢ,εₖ)=0 for i≠k, and Var(εᵢ)=xᵢ²σ². The xᵢ are fixed and nonzero. Which expression is the best linear unbiased estimator of β?
items.explanation: The error variance is not constant: Var(εᵢ)=xᵢ²σ². Divide the model by xᵢ: Yᵢ/xᵢ=β+εᵢ/xᵢ. The transformed errors εᵢ/xᵢ have mean zero, are uncorrelated, and each has variance Var(εᵢ/xᵢ)=xᵢ²σ²/xᵢ²=σ². Thus the transformed model has a common error variance and a constant mean β. The least-squares estimator of this common mean is the average of the transformed observations: β̂=(1/n)∑(Yᵢ/xᵢ). By the Gauss–Markov theorem applied to the transformed model, this is BLUE. Hence option 3 is correct. Other-exam relevance: weighted least squares, heteroscedasticity and BLUE are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi; This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · diagonal elements of the hat matrix and leverage bounds
items.stem: Consider a simple linear regression model yᵢ=α+βxᵢ+εᵢ based on n=50 observations, where not all xᵢ are equal. Which of the following is an admissible value of the leverage of the 11th observation?
items.explanation:
In simple linear regression with an intercept, the leverage of observation i is the diagonal element hᵢᵢ of the hat matrix. Its formula is hᵢᵢ=1/n+(xᵢ−x̄)²/∑ⱼ(xⱼ−x̄)².

Step 1: The first term is 1/n=1/50=0.02. The second term is a square divided by a sum of squares, so it is nonnegative. Therefore every leverage satisfies hᵢᵢ≥0.02. This rules out 0 and 0.01.

Step 2: A diagonal element of the projection (hat) matrix cannot exceed 1. Equivalently, the leverage values are nonnegative and their sum is the model rank, which is 2 here. Thus 1.1 is impossible.

Step 3: The value 0.1 lies between the lower and upper bounds. It is attainable: it requires (x₁₁−x̄)²/Sxx=0.1−0.02=0.08, a feasible share of the total centred sum of squares for a sample of 50 observations.

Hence 0.1, option C, is admissible. The important exam shortcut is that with one predictor and an intercept, the minimum leverage is 1/n, not zero. Other-exam relevance: the hat matrix, leverage and influence diagnostics are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: multivariate-t2 · multiple correlation with equicorrelated predictors
items.stem: Let p>1 and 1>ρ≥0. In a multiple regression setting, suppose the correlation between Y and each predictor Xᵢ is ρ, and the correlation between every pair of distinct predictors Xᵢ and Xⱼ is also ρ. Which statements about the multiple correlation coefficient R between Y and (X₁,…,Xₚ) are correct?
statements: R is greater than or equal to ρ.
R equals ρ when ρ=0.
R equals ρ only when ρ=0.
R tends to 1 as p tends to infinity.

A.why: The squared multiple correlation is R²=pρ²/[1+(p−1)ρ]. For 0≤ρ<1 this gives R≥ρ; equality occurs at ρ=0.

B.why: When ρ=0, the correlation vector between Y and all predictors is zero, so R=0=ρ.

C.why: For ρ>0 and ρ<1, p/[1+(p−1)ρ] is greater than one, so R>ρ. Equality is therefore possible only at ρ=0 under the stated parameter range.

D.why: For fixed ρ, R² tends to ρ as p grows, so R tends to √ρ, not 1 unless ρ=1. The question restricts ρ<1.

items.explanation:
The multiple correlation coefficient R measures how strongly Y is linearly related to the whole set of predictors taken together. We can calculate it from the predictor correlation matrix.

Step 1: The p predictors have pairwise correlation ρ, so their correlation matrix is Rₓ=(1−ρ)I+ρJ, where I is the identity matrix and J is the matrix of ones. The vector of correlations between Y and the p predictors is r=ρ·1.

Step 2: The squared multiple correlation is R²=r′Rₓ⁻¹r. The vector of ones is an eigenvector of Rₓ with eigenvalue 1+(p−1)ρ. Therefore Rₓ⁻¹1=1/[1+(p−1)ρ]·1.

Step 3: Substitute r=ρ·1:
R²=ρ²·1′Rₓ⁻¹1=ρ²·p/[1+(p−1)ρ]. Hence R=ρ√[p/{1+(p−1)ρ}], since ρ≥0.

Step 4: Because 0≤ρ<1, we have 1+(p−1)ρ≤p. Thus the square-root factor is at least one and R≥ρ. If ρ=0, then R=0=ρ. If ρ>0, the denominator is strictly less than p, so R>ρ. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are true.

Step 5: For fixed ρ, as p→∞, R²→ρ and therefore R→√ρ. Since the question states ρ<1, this limit is below one (unless the excluded boundary ρ=1 is considered). Statement 4 is false.

Therefore statements 1, 2 and 3 only are correct: option A. Other-exam relevance: multiple correlation, predictor correlation matrices and multicollinearity are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

Source-key audit: the supplied answer key lists only statements 1 and 2. However, statement 3 is also logically true: under 0≤ρ<1, equality R=ρ occurs at ρ=0; for ρ>0 the square-root factor is strictly greater than one. Thus the phrase “R equals ρ only if ρ=0” is correct. The bank therefore uses statements 1, 2 and 3 only, rather than reproducing the incomplete printed key.

items.topic: regression-t7 · generalized least squares and BLUE under known heteroscedastic variances
items.stem: Consider Yᵢ=iβ+εᵢ, i=1,2,3, where the independent errors have mean zero and variances σ², 2σ² and 3σ², respectively. What is the BLUE of β?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 77 (June 2015), page 40. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists C. The model is through the origin with design values xᵢ=i and known error variances Var(εᵢ)=iσ². Generalised least squares gives β̂=[ΣxᵢYᵢ/Var(εᵢ)]/[Σxᵢ²/Var(εᵢ)]. Since xᵢ=i and Var(εᵢ)=iσ², the numerator is ΣYᵢ/σ² and the denominator is Σi/σ²=6/σ². Thus β̂=(Y₁+Y₂+Y₃)/6, option C. GLS is the BLUE because it uses inverse-variance weights; ordinary least squares is not efficient under these unequal variances. Other-exam relevance: GLS, heteroscedasticity and BLUE overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Printed answer-key cross-check (source PDF page 64): Q77 is listed as C.

items.topic: regression-t7 · BLUE and variance estimation under heteroscedastic scaled observations
items.stem: Let Y₁,…,Yₙ be uncorrelated with E(Yᵢ)=iθ and Var(Yᵢ)=i²σ². Define T₁=(1/n)Σ(Yᵢ/i) and T₂=[6/{n(n+1)(2n+1)}]ΣiYᵢ. Which statements are true?
statements: T₁ is the BLUE of θ.
T₂ is the ordinary least-squares estimator of θ in the model Yᵢ=iθ+εᵢ.
Var(T₁)=σ²/n.
An unbiased estimator of σ² is [Σ(Yᵢ/i)²−(1/n)(ΣYᵢ/i)²]/(n−1).

A.why: Zᵢ=Yᵢ/i are uncorrelated with common mean θ and common variance σ²; their average is the BLUE.

B.why: OLS through the origin gives ΣiYᵢ/Σi², and Σi²=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, exactly T₂.

C.why: Each Zᵢ has variance σ², so the variance of their average is σ²/n.

D.why: The displayed expression is the usual sample variance of Zᵢ=Yᵢ/i and is unbiased for σ².

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 85 (December 2013), page 46. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists A,B,C,D. Put Zᵢ=Yᵢ/i. Then E(Zᵢ)=θ and Var(Zᵢ)=σ², and the Zᵢ are uncorrelated. Their average T₁ is unbiased with variance σ²/n; equal weights minimise variance among linear unbiased combinations, so T₁ is BLUE. For the original regression through the origin, OLS minimises Σ(Yᵢ−iθ)². Differentiating gives θ̂_OLS=ΣiYᵢ/Σi². Since Σi²=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, this is T₂. Finally, the usual sample variance of Z₁,…,Zₙ is [ΣZᵢ²−(1/n)(ΣZᵢ)²]/(n−1), unbiased for σ²; substituting Zᵢ=Yᵢ/i gives statement D. All four statements are true, option D. Other-exam relevance: BLUE, OLS, heteroscedasticity and unbiased variance estimation overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Printed answer-key cross-check (source PDF page 64): Q85 is listed as A,B,C,D.

items.topic: regression-t2 · BLUE and ordinary least squares for a common mean with equicorrelated covariance structure
items.stem: Let Y₁,…,Yₙ have a common unknown mean θ. The inverse of their variance-covariance matrix has all diagonal elements equal to c and all off-diagonal elements equal to d. Let T₁ be the BLUE of θ and T₂ the ordinary least-squares estimator. Which statements are true?
statements: T₁=(1/n)ΣYᵢ=T₂.
T₂=nȲ and T₁=Σ(Yᵢ−Ȳ).
There are exactly n−1 linearly independent linear functions of Y₁,…,Yₙ, each with zero expectation.
There are exactly n−2 linearly independent linear functions of Y₁,…,Yₙ, each with zero expectation.

A.why: The equal row sums of the inverse covariance matrix make the GLS weights equal, so the BLUE is the ordinary mean; OLS for a common mean is also the ordinary mean.

B.why: The OLS estimator is Ȳ, not nȲ, and the stated expression for T₁ is not the BLUE.

C.why: A linear function aᵀY has expectation θΣaᵢ. It has zero expectation exactly when Σaᵢ=0, a subspace of dimension n−1.

D.why: The zero-sum coefficient subspace has dimension n−1, not n−2.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 75 (December 2015), page 39. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists A and C. For a common mean, the GLS estimator is [1ᵀV⁻¹Y]/[1ᵀV⁻¹1]. Since V⁻¹ has the same diagonal value c and same off-diagonal value d, every row sum is c+(n−1)d. Thus V⁻¹1 is proportional to 1, and the GLS weights are equal. Therefore T₁=Ȳ. Ordinary least squares for a common mean also gives T₂=Ȳ, so A is true. A linear function aᵀY has expectation θΣaᵢ. It has zero expectation for every θ precisely when the coefficients sum to zero. This is one linear restriction on n coefficients, leaving a subspace of dimension n−1. Hence C is true and D false. B is false because it does not give the OLS and BLUE expressions correctly. Answer A and C only. Other-exam relevance: GLS, BLUE, covariance structures and linear unbiased estimation overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · estimability and BLUE under a partially specified covariance structure
items.stem: Let Y₁,Y₂,Y₃,Y₄ have expectations E(Y₁)=θ₁−θ₃, E(Y₂)=θ₁+θ₂−θ₃, E(Y₃)=θ₁−θ₃ and E(Y₄)=θ₁−θ₂−θ₃, where θ₁,θ₂,θ₃ are unknown. Suppose Var(Yᵢ)=σ² for i=1,2,3,4. No covariances are specified. Which statements are guaranteed by the printed assumptions?
statements: θ₁, θ₂ and θ₃ are all estimable.
θ₁+θ₃ is estimable.
θ₁−θ₃ is estimable and (Y₁+Y₃)/2 is its BLUE.
θ₂ is estimable.

A.why: The expectations identify θ₁−θ₃ and θ₂, but not θ₁ and θ₃ separately.

B.why: The coefficient vector for θ₁+θ₃ is not in the row space of the expectation design matrix.

C.why: θ₁−θ₃ is estimable, but the claim that (Y₁+Y₃)/2 is BLUE needs Cov(Y₁,Y₃)=0 (or another covariance condition). The question gives only marginal variances, so this BLUE claim is not guaranteed.

D.why: E[(Y₂−Y₄)/2]=[(θ₁+θ₂−θ₃)−(θ₁−θ₂−θ₃)]/2=θ₂, so θ₂ is estimable.

items.explanation: The printed answer key on PDF page 65 lists statement C only. Check the expectation equations directly. First, E(Y₁)=E(Y₃)=θ₁−θ₃, so θ₁−θ₃ is estimable. Also E[(Y₂−Y₄)/2]=θ₂, so statement D is definitely true. The individual parameters θ₁ and θ₃ cannot be separated, and θ₁+θ₃ is not identified by these four expectations, so A and B are false. Statement C contains two claims: the contrast θ₁−θ₃ is estimable, but the assertion that (Y₁+Y₃)/2 is BLUE requires a covariance assumption. Its variance is [2σ²+2Cov(Y₁,Y₃)]/4, and the question does not specify Cov(Y₁,Y₃) or any other off-diagonal covariance. Thus C is not guaranteed by the literal printed assumptions. The mathematically guaranteed statement is D only. The key's C-only answer conflicts with the estimability of θ₂ and also assumes information about covariances that is not printed. Treat this as a flawed-source item: do not memorise the key without noting the missing assumptions. Other-exam relevance: estimability, row-space conditions and BLUE calculations overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · maximum likelihood for a finite-support discrete distribution
items.stem: A random variable has probability mass function P(X=0)=(1−θ)/2, P(X=1)=1/2 and P(X=2)=θ/2, where 0<θ<1. In a random sample of size 100, the observed counts at 0, 1 and 2 are 20, 30 and 50, respectively. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of θ?
items.explanation:
Let n₀=20, n₁=30 and n₂=50. The likelihood is the product of the probabilities raised to their observed counts:

L(θ)=[(1−θ)/2]²⁰(1/2)³⁰(θ/2)⁵⁰. All powers of 1/2 are constant with respect to θ, so we only need to maximise θ⁵⁰(1−θ)²⁰ for 0<θ<1.

Take the logarithm: ℓ(θ)=50 ln θ+20 ln(1−θ)+constant. Differentiate: ℓ′(θ)=50/θ−20/(1−θ). Set this equal to zero: 50(1−θ)=20θ, so 50=70θ and θ̂=50/70=5/7. The log-likelihood is strictly concave, so this stationary point is the unique maximum. The answer is option 2 (B), matching the supplied answer key on page 53.

Other-exam relevance: likelihood maximisation for a discrete parametric model is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 77, June 2024, page 46; answer key page 53.

items.topic: inference-t13 · chi-square pivot and a one-sided confidence interval for a normal variance
items.stem: Let X₁ and X₂ be a random sample from N(0,σ²), where σ>0 is unknown. Suppose that (c(X₁²+X₂²),∞) is a confidence interval for σ² with confidence coefficient 0.95. What is c?
items.explanation:
Because X₁ and X₂ are independent N(0,σ²), the standard chi-square result gives (X₁²+X₂²)/σ² ~ χ² with 2 degrees of freedom. Let T=(X₁²+X₂²)/σ². The proposed interval contains the true σ² when c(X₁²+X₂²)≤σ², which is equivalent to cT≤1, or T≤1/c.

For a chi-square variable with 2 degrees of freedom, its cumulative distribution function is F(t)=1−e^(−t/2), for t≥0. We need P(T≤1/c)=0.95. Thus 1−exp[−1/(2c)]=0.95, so exp[−1/(2c)]=0.05. Taking logarithms gives 1/(2c)=−ln(0.05), hence c=1/[−2 ln(0.05)]. The answer is option 3 (C), matching the supplied answer key on page 53.

Other-exam relevance: chi-square pivots and confidence intervals for normal variance are useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics. items.topic: regression-t4 · regression R-squared and residual sum of squares from standardised variables
items.stem: Suppose C, S and TI are standardised sample variables, each with sample mean 0 and sample variance 1, with covariances and variances computed using divisor 20. Let DI=C+S. The slopes in the simple regressions of DI on TI, DI on C, and S on TI are 0.8, 0.5 and 0.4, respectively. There are 21 observations. What is the residual sum of squares in the regression of DI on S?
items.explanation:
The sample variances of C and S are both 1. The slope in the regression of DI on C is Cov(DI,C)/Var(C). Since DI=C+S, this slope is [Var(C)+Cov(S,C)]/1=0.5. Therefore Cov(S,C)=−0.5.

Now calculate the variance of DI: Var(DI)=Var(C+S)=Var(C)+Var(S)+2Cov(C,S)=1+1+2(−0.5)=1. The covariance between DI and S is Cov(C+S,S)=Cov(C,S)+Var(S)=−0.5+1=0.5. Hence the regression slope of DI on S is 0.5, and its coefficient of determination is R²=Cov(DI,S)²/[Var(DI)Var(S)]=(0.5)²/(1×1)=0.25.

With 21 observations and sample variances defined using divisor 20, the total sum of squares for DI is 20×Var(DI)=20. Therefore SSE=(1−R²)SST=(1−0.25)×20=15. The answer is option 3 (C), matching the supplied answer key on page 53.

items.topic: inference-t4 · inference-t5 · maximum likelihood and method of moments for a uniform location-scale family
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ, n≥2, be a random sample from Uniform(−θ,2θ), where θ>0 is unknown. Write X̄ for the sample mean, X₍₁₎=min(X₁,…,Xₙ) and X₍ₙ₎=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which statements are true?
statements: The maximum-likelihood estimator of θ is min{X₍₁₎, X₍ₙ₎/2}.
The maximum-likelihood estimator of θ is max{−X₍₁₎, X₍ₙ₎/2}.
The method-of-moments estimator of θ is 2X̄.
The method-of-moments estimator of θ is 2X̄/3.

A.why: The likelihood is positive only when θ is at least −X₍₁₎ and at least X₍ₙ₎/2. The minimum admissible value is their maximum, not their minimum.

B.why: The density is 1/(3θ) on [−θ,2θ]. The likelihood is proportional to θ⁻ⁿ on the admissible parameter set, so it is maximised at θ̂=max{−X₍₁₎,X₍ₙ₎/2}.

C.why: The population mean of Uniform(−θ,2θ) is [−θ+2θ]/2=θ/2. Equating X̄ to θ/2 gives θ̂MM=2X̄.

D.why: The population mean is θ/2, not 3θ/2, so the method-of-moments equation does not give 2X̄/3.

items.explanation:
For a Uniform(−θ,2θ) distribution, the density is 1/(3θ) when every observation lies between −θ and 2θ, and is zero otherwise. The likelihood is therefore L(θ)=(3θ)⁻ⁿ provided θ≥−X₍₁₎ and θ≥X₍ₙ₎/2. Outside this range the likelihood is zero. Within the allowed range, (3θ)⁻ⁿ decreases as θ increases. So we choose the smallest allowed value: θ̂MLE=max{−X₍₁₎,X₍ₙ₎/2}. Statement 2 is true.

For the method of moments, first find the population mean. A uniform distribution on [a,b] has mean (a+b)/2. Here a=−θ and b=2θ, so E(X)=θ/2. Equating this to the sample mean gives X̄=θ/2 and θ̂MM=2X̄. Statement 3 is true. Therefore statements 2 and 3 only are correct. The four combination options are editorially supplied to make the source's statement-selection format usable in the bank; the supplied key lists statements 2 and 3 on page 53.

items.topic: inference-t4 · likelihood for a mixture distribution generated by a Bernoulli variable
items.stem: Let X and Y be independent, where X~Uniform(0,1) and Y~Bernoulli(p), 0<p<1. Define Z=X+Y. Six independent observations from Z are 0.5, 1.2, 1.3, 0.9, 0.1 and 0.7. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of p?
items.explanation:
If Y=0, then Z=X lies between 0 and 1. If Y=1, then Z=X+1 lies between 1 and 2. Therefore an observed value below 1 comes from Y=0, while a value above 1 comes from Y=1 (the probability of observing exactly 1 is zero).

Among the six observations, 1.2 and 1.3 are above 1, so there are 2 observations from the shifted component. The other 4 observations are below 1. The likelihood for p is therefore proportional to p²(1−p)⁴. The log-likelihood is ℓ(p)=2 ln p+4 ln(1−p)+constant. Differentiating and setting to zero gives 2/p−4/(1−p)=0, so 2(1−p)=4p and p̂=2/6=1/3. The second derivative is negative, confirming a maximum. The answer is option 3 (C), matching the supplied answer key on page 53.

items.topic: inference-t13 · confidence coefficient from a pivotal distribution
items.stem: A random variable X has density f(x|θ)=2(θ−x)/θ² for 0≤x≤θ and zero otherwise, where θ>0 is unknown. Based on one observation X, what is the confidence coefficient of the interval [2X/5, 5X/2] for θ?
items.explanation:
Set U=X/θ. Using the density of X and the change of variable x=θu, the density of U is f_U(u)=2(1−u), for 0≤u≤1. The interval [2X/5,5X/2] contains θ when both inequalities hold. The lower-end inequality 2X/5≤θ is always true because X≤θ. The upper-end inequality θ≤5X/2 is equivalent to X/θ≥2/5, or U≥0.4.

Therefore the confidence coefficient is P(U≥0.4)=∫₀.₄¹2(1−u)du=[2u−u²]₀.₄¹=1−(0.8−0.16)=0.36. The answer is option 1 (A), matching the supplied answer key on page 53.

items.topic: inference-t4 · maximum likelihood and method of moments for a logistic Bernoulli parameterisation
items.stem: Let X₁,…,X₁₀ be a random sample from a Bernoulli distribution with success probability p(θ)=1/(1+e^θ), where θ∈ℝ is unknown. Let M=Σᵢ₌₁¹⁰Xᵢ. Which statements are true?
statements: When M=0, a finite maximum-likelihood estimate of θ exists and equals 0.
When M=10, a finite maximum-likelihood estimate of θ does not exist.
For M∈{1,…,9}, the maximum-likelihood estimate exists and equals ln(10/M−1).
The method-of-moments estimate of θ is M/10.

A.why: When M=0, the likelihood is (1−p(θ))¹⁰ and approaches its supremum as θ→−∞; no finite θ attains it.

B.why: When M=10, the likelihood is p(θ)¹⁰ and approaches its supremum as θ→−∞; no finite θ attains it.

C.why: For 1≤M≤9, differentiating the log-likelihood gives e^θ=(10−M)/M, so θ̂=ln(10/M−1).

D.why: The sample mean estimates p, not θ. Equating M/10 to 1/(1+e^θ) and solving gives the same log-odds expression as in statement 3, not M/10.

items.explanation:
Write p(θ)=1/(1+e^θ). The likelihood based on M successes and 10−M failures is L(θ)=p(θ)^M[1−p(θ)]^(10−M).

If M=0, then L(θ)=[1−p(θ)]¹⁰. As θ tends to −∞, p(θ) tends to 1 and this likelihood tends to 0; as θ tends to +∞, p(θ) tends to 0 and the likelihood tends to 1. The supremum is approached but is not attained at any finite θ, so statement 1 is false. If M=10, L(θ)=p(θ)¹⁰, which tends to 1 as θ tends to −∞ but never reaches 1 for finite θ. Thus a finite MLE does not exist and statement 2 is true.

For 1≤M≤9, differentiate the log-likelihood. Setting the derivative to zero gives e^θ=(10−M)/M, hence θ̂=ln(10/M−1); statement 3 is true. For method of moments, M/10 estimates the Bernoulli probability p. Solving M/10=1/(1+e^θ) gives θ̂MM=ln(10/M−1), not M/10, so statement 4 is false. Therefore statements 2 and 3 only are correct. The combination choices are editorially supplied; the source key lists statements 2 and 3 on page 53.

items.topic: inference-t4 · maximum likelihood with parameter-dependent uniform support
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ, n≥2, be a random sample from Uniform(θ,1−θ), where −∞<θ<1/2. What is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ?
items.explanation:
Let X₍₁₎ be the sample minimum and X₍ₙ₎ the sample maximum. The density is 1/(1−2θ) when every observation lies in [θ,1−θ], and zero otherwise. The likelihood is therefore L(θ)=(1−2θ)⁻ⁿ subject to θ≤X₍₁₎ and θ≤1−X₍ₙ₎. These support restrictions combine to θ≤min{X₍₁₎,1−X₍ₙ₎}.

Within the allowed parameter range, 1−2θ decreases as θ increases, so (1−2θ)⁻ⁿ increases as θ increases. The likelihood is maximised by taking θ as large as the support constraints permit. Thus θ̂MLE=min{X₍₁₎,1−X₍ₙ₎}, which is option 3 (C). This agrees with the supplied answer key on page 53.

items.topic: inference-t13 · confidence intervals from the minimum of shifted exponential observations
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from the density f(x|θ)=e^{−(x−θ)} for x≥θ and zero otherwise, where θ∈ℝ is unknown. Let X₍₁₎=min(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which statements give the stated confidence coefficient for θ?
statements: (X₍₁₎−(2/n)ln 5, X₍₁₎) has confidence coefficient 0.97.
(X₍₁₎−(2/n)ln 5, X₍₁₎) has confidence coefficient 0.96.
(X₍₁₎−(1/n)ln 20, X₍₁₎) has confidence coefficient 0.95.
(X₍₁₎−(1/n)ln 20, X₍₁₎) has confidence coefficient 0.96.

A.why: The coverage for the first interval is 1−exp[−n(2 ln 5/n)]=1−1/25=0.96, not 0.97.

B.why: The first interval has coefficient 0.96, and the second has coefficient 1−exp(−ln 20)=0.95.

C.why: For c=(1/n)ln 20, the coverage is 1−exp(−ln 20)=0.95, so statement 3 is true.

D.why: Statement 4 is false because the interval in statement 3 has coefficient 0.95, not 0.96.

items.explanation:
The minimum of n independent shifted exponential observations has the form X₍₁₎=θ+E, where E is exponential with rate n. Thus P(E≤c)=1−e^(−nc). For an interval (X₍₁₎−c,X₍₁₎), the true θ is always below X₍₁₎, and it is above the lower endpoint exactly when E≤c. Therefore the confidence coefficient is 1−e^(−nc).

For c=(2/n)ln 5, the coefficient is 1−e^(−2 ln 5)=1−1/25=24/25=0.96. So statement 2 is true and statement 1 is false. For c=(1/n)ln 20, the coefficient is 1−e^(−ln 20)=1−1/20=0.95. So statement 3 is true and statement 4 is false. Therefore statements 2 and 3 only are correct. The combination options are editorially supplied; the supplied answer key lists statements 2 and 3 on page 53.

items.topic: inference-t4 · maximum likelihood for a finite-support discrete distribution
items.stem: A discrete random variable X has probabilities P(X=0)=θ/3, P(X=1)=1−θ/2 and P(X=2)=θ/6, where 0<θ<1. In a sample of size 90, the observed counts at 0, 1 and 2 are 20, 60 and 10, respectively. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of θ?
items.explanation:
The likelihood is proportional to (θ/3)²⁰(1−θ/2)⁶⁰(θ/6)¹⁰. Terms that do not depend on θ can be ignored, leaving L(θ)∝θ³⁰(1−θ/2)⁶⁰.

Take logarithms: ℓ(θ)=30 ln θ+60 ln(1−θ/2)+constant. Differentiate: ℓ′(θ)=30/θ−30/(1−θ/2). Set this equal to zero: 30/θ=30/(1−θ/2), so θ=1−θ/2. Hence 3θ/2=1 and θ̂=2/3. The log-likelihood is concave on the parameter interval, so this is the maximum. The answer is option 3 (C), matching the supplied answer key on page 53.

items.topic: inference-t13 · confidence intervals using a transformed pivotal variable
items.stem: Let X have density f(x|θ)=3(θ−x)²/θ³ for 0<x<θ and zero otherwise. For λ₁,λ₂∈(0,1), λ₁<λ₂, consider the interval (X/(1−λ₁), X/(1−λ₂)). Which condition makes its confidence coefficient equal to 1−α?
items.explanation:
Let U=X/θ. Using x=θu in the density, U has density f_U(u)=3(1−u)² for 0<u<1. Its cumulative distribution function is F_U(u)=1−(1−u)³.

The interval contains θ when X/(1−λ₁)<θ<X/(1−λ₂). Dividing by θ and using U=X/θ gives 1−λ₂<U<1−λ₁. Therefore its coverage probability is F_U(1−λ₁)−F_U(1−λ₂). Substitute the CDF: [1−λ₁³]−[1−λ₂³]=λ₂³−λ₁³. For the confidence coefficient to be 1−α, we require λ₂³−λ₁³=1−α. This is option 2 (B), matching the supplied answer key on page 53.

items.topic: inference-t7 · Bayesian estimation with an improper flat prior in the normal location model
items.stem: Suppose X|θ~N(θ,15), and the prior density for θ is proportional to 1 on the real line. If the observed value is X=13, which statement is true?
options: The posterior mean equals the maximum-likelihood estimate of θ, and the posterior variance equals Var(X|θ).
The posterior mean equals the maximum-likelihood estimate of θ, and the posterior variance is smaller than Var(X|θ).
The posterior mean is greater than the maximum-likelihood estimate of θ, and the posterior variance equals Var(X|θ).
The posterior mean is greater than the maximum-likelihood estimate of θ, and the posterior variance is smaller than Var(X|θ).
items.explanation:
The likelihood as a function of θ is proportional to exp[−(13−θ)²/(2×15)]. The prior is flat, so multiplying by the prior does not change this kernel. After normalisation, the posterior distribution is N(13,15).

The posterior mean is therefore 13. The maximum-likelihood estimate in the normal location model is also the observed value, 13. The posterior variance is 15, which is exactly the sampling variance Var(X|θ)=15. Thus the posterior mean equals the MLE and the posterior variance equals the sampling variance. Option 1 (A) is correct, matching the supplied answer key on page 53. The flat prior is improper, but the resulting posterior is proper because the normal likelihood has a finite integral over θ.

items.topic: inference-t13 · confidence intervals from the minimum of shifted exponential observations
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. with density f(x|θ)=e^{−(x−θ)} for x≥θ and zero otherwise, where θ∈ℝ is unknown. Let Y=min(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which of the following intervals have confidence coefficient 1−α?

A.why: Statement 1 does not have coverage 1−α; its coverage is α/2.

B.why: Statement 2 does not have coverage 1−α; its coverage is 1−√α.

C.why: Statement 3 has coverage (1−α/2)²−(α/2)²=1−α.

D.why: Statement 4 has coverage (1−α/2)−(α/2)=1−α.

items.explanation:
The minimum Y has the distribution Y=θ+E, where E is exponential with rate n. Thus for 0≤a<b, P(a≤E≤b)=e^(−na)−e^(−nb). A confidence interval for θ can be obtained by choosing constants so that the probability that θ lies between its two endpoints is 1−α.

For statement 3, the endpoints are Y+(2/n)ln(α/2) and Y+(2/n)ln(1−α/2). Both logarithms are negative. The event that θ lies in this interval is equivalent to −(2/n)ln(1−α/2)≤E≤−(2/n)ln(α/2). Its probability is (1−α/2)²−(α/2)²=1−α. So statement 3 is correct.

For statement 4, the same calculation with 1/n instead of 2/n gives probability (1−α/2)−(α/2)=1−α. So statement 4 is also correct. Statement 1 gives only α/2 coverage, and statement 2 gives 1−√α coverage, so neither is generally 1−α. Therefore statements 3 and 4 only are correct, matching the supplied answer key on page 53. The combination choices are editorially supplied because the scan lists four candidate intervals without combination options.

items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t5 · sufficiency, unbiased estimation and method of moments for a Poisson model
items.stem: Let X₁,…,X₁₃ be i.i.d. Poisson(θ), θ>0. Which of the following statements are true?
statements: (Σᵢ₌₁⁸Xᵢ)(Σᵢ₌₈¹³Xᵢ) is an unbiased estimator of 48θ².
(1/13)Σᵢ₌₁¹³Xᵢ is the method-of-moments estimator of θ.
There does not exist any unbiased estimator of e^(−7θ).
(e^(X₇), Σᵢ₌₁⁶Xᵢ, Σᵢ₌₈¹³Xᵢ) is a sufficient statistic for θ.

A.why: The two sums share X₈. Their product has expectation 48θ²+θ, not 48θ².

B.why: Since E(Xᵢ)=θ, the sample mean has expectation θ and is the method-of-moments estimator.

C.why: The indicator that X₁=…=X₇=0 has expectation P(X₁=…=X₇=0)=e^(−7θ), so an unbiased estimator does exist.

D.why: The exponential function is one-to-one, so e^(X₇) determines X₇. Together with the two sums, the statistic determines Σᵢ₌₁¹³Xᵢ, which is sufficient for θ in an i.i.d. Poisson sample.

items.explanation:
Check each statement using expectation and the Poisson likelihood.

Statement 1 is false because the two sums overlap at X₈. Write A=Σᵢ₌₁⁸Xᵢ and B=Σᵢ₌₈¹³Xᵢ. Then E(A)=8θ, E(B)=6θ and Cov(A,B)=Var(X₈)=θ. Hence E(AB)=E(A)E(B)+Cov(A,B)=48θ²+θ, not 48θ².

Statement 2 is true. For a Poisson(θ) variable, E(X)=θ. Equating the population mean to the sample mean gives θ̂MM=X̄=(1/13)ΣXᵢ.

Statement 3 is false. Define T=1{X₁=0,…,X₇=0}. By independence, E(T)=P(X₁=0,…,X₇=0)=(e^(−θ))⁷=e^(−7θ). Thus T is an unbiased estimator of e^(−7θ).

Statement 4 is true. Since e^(X₇) uniquely determines X₇, the displayed statistic determines X₇+Σᵢ₌₁⁶Xᵢ+Σᵢ₌₈¹³Xᵢ=Σᵢ₌₁¹³Xᵢ. The total sum is sufficient for θ in an i.i.d. Poisson sample, so the displayed statistic is also sufficient. Therefore statements 2 and 4 only are true, option B.

**Printed-key discrepancy:** the supplied answer-key page 53 lists statements 1 and 3. Both conflict with the literal printed question: statement 1 omits the covariance contribution from the shared X₈, and statement 3 is disproved by the seven-zero indicator estimator. The bank records the mathematically derived answer and preserves this discrepancy visibly. The scan's source wording has been retained; no unstated independence between the overlapping sums has been assumed.

items.topic: regression-t2 · OLS normal equations and residual properties with versus without an intercept
items.stem: Let {(xᵢ,yᵢ): i=1,2,…,n} be given data points, where the xᵢ are not all equal. Analyst C fits a linear regression of y on x with an intercept, while analyst D fits a linear regression of y on x without an intercept. Let x̄ and ȳ be the sample means of x and y. Which of the following statements are NOT necessarily true?
statements: Both fitted regression lines will pass through the point (x̄,ȳ).
C's fitted line will pass through (x̄,ȳ), but D's fitted line will not pass through (x̄,ȳ).
For both fitted models, the sample correlation coefficient between x and the corresponding residuals is zero.
The sample correlation coefficient between x and the corresponding residuals is zero for C's fitted model, but is not guaranteed to be zero for D's fitted model.

A.why: The no-intercept fit is constrained to pass through the origin; it is not generally constrained to pass through (x̄,ȳ).

B.why: The no-intercept line can pass through (x̄,ȳ) for some data sets, so the word 'will not' is too strong.

C.why: With an intercept, residuals are orthogonal to both the constant and x, giving zero sample correlation (when defined). Without an intercept, only Σxᵢeᵢ=0 is guaranteed, not centered covariance zero.

D.why: This is the intended general contrast: the intercept model guarantees zero sample correlation, whereas the no-intercept normal equations do not guarantee it. The phrase 'but not for D' is read as 'not guaranteed for D', rather than 'always nonzero for D'.

items.explanation:
The key difference is the OLS normal equations.

**Model C: regression with an intercept.** Its residuals eᵢ satisfy Σeᵢ=0 and Σxᵢeᵢ=0. The first equation says the fitted residuals average to zero. Together with the second, it gives the fitted line passing through (x̄,ȳ). It also gives zero centered sample covariance between x and the residuals, so their sample correlation is zero whenever that correlation is defined.

**Model D: regression without an intercept.** Its only slope normal equation is Σxᵢeᵢ=0. There is no normal equation requiring Σeᵢ=0. Therefore the fitted line need not pass through (x̄,ȳ), and the centered covariance between x and residuals is not forced to be zero. It can be zero for special data sets, but is not guaranteed to be zero.

Thus statements 1, 2 and 3 are not necessarily true, while statement 4 expresses the intended contrast. **Wording note:** statement 4 is potentially ambiguous if 'but not for D' is read as 'the correlation is always nonzero for D'. The source answer key (page 51) treats it as 'not guaranteed to be zero for D'; the bank makes that intended reading explicit rather than asserting universal nonzero correlation.

items.topic: multivariate-t7 · maximum likelihood estimation of the correlation in a bivariate normal model with equal marginal variances
items.stem: Let (X₁,Y₁),…,(Xₙ,Yₙ), n≥4, be a random sample from a bivariate normal distribution with E(Xᵢ)=μ₁, E(Yᵢ)=μ₂, Var(Xᵢ)=Var(Yᵢ)=σ² and correlation coefficient ρ. All four parameters μ₁, μ₂, σ² and ρ are unknown. Define Sₓₓ=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ(Xᵢ−X̄)², Sᵧᵧ=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ(Yᵢ−Ȳ)² and Sₓᵧ=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ(Xᵢ−X̄)(Yᵢ−Ȳ). Which expression is the maximum-likelihood estimator of ρ?
items.explanation:
Because the two marginal variances are constrained to be equal, the covariance matrix is σ²[[1,ρ],[ρ,1]]. The unknown means are estimated by X̄ and Ȳ, so the likelihood can be written using the centred sums Sₓₓ, Sᵧᵧ and Sₓᵧ.

After maximising over σ², the part of the profile log-likelihood that depends on ρ is proportional to −n log(Sₓₓ+Sᵧᵧ−2ρSₓᵧ)+(n/2)log(1−ρ²). Differentiate with respect to ρ and set the derivative to zero:

2Sₓᵧ/(Sₓₓ+Sᵧᵧ−2ρSₓᵧ) − ρ/(1−ρ²)=0.

Cross-multiplying gives 2Sₓᵧ(1−ρ²)=ρ(Sₓₓ+Sᵧᵧ−2ρSₓᵧ). The terms −2ρ²Sₓᵧ cancel on both sides, leaving 2Sₓᵧ=ρ(Sₓₓ+Sᵧᵧ). Hence ρ̂=2Sₓᵧ/(Sₓₓ+Sᵧᵧ), option 3 (C). This differs from the ordinary sample correlation Sₓᵧ/√(SₓₓSᵧᵧ), because the model imposes equal marginal variances and estimates ρ jointly with the common variance. The supplied answer key on page 51 lists option 3.

items.topic: inference-t13 · exact confidence intervals from a scaled uniform distribution
items.stem: Let X have density f(x|θ)=2x/θ² for 0<x<θ and zero otherwise, where θ>0 is unknown. Which of the following are 100(1−α)% confidence intervals for θ?

A.why: For U=X/θ, P(U≥√α)=1−α, so interval 1 has the required confidence coefficient.

B.why: Interval 2 has coverage 3/4, not 1−α for general α.

C.why: The event is √(α/2)≤U≤√((2−α)/2), whose probability is 1−α.

D.why: Intervals 2 and 4 do not have the required confidence coefficient.

items.explanation:
Start by finding the distribution of U=X/θ. Since X has density 2x/θ² on (0,θ), a change of variable gives f_U(u)=2u for 0<u<1. Hence F_U(u)=u².

For interval 1, [X,X/√α], the lower endpoint is always below θ because X<θ. The upper endpoint is at least θ exactly when X/√α≥θ, or U≥√α. Therefore the coverage is P(U≥√α)=1−F_U(√α)=1−α.

For interval 2, [X,2X], coverage requires U≥1/2, so its coverage is 1−(1/2)²=3/4. It is not a general 1−α interval.

For interval 3, let a=√(2/(2−α)) and b=√(2/α). The event aX≤θ≤bX is equivalent to 1/b≤U≤1/a. Its probability is (1/a)²−(1/b)²=(2−α)/2−α/2=1−α. Thus interval 3 is also correct.

Interval 4, [0,X], cannot contain θ because X<θ almost surely. Therefore statements 1 and 3 only are correct. The supplied answer key on page 51 lists statements 1 and 3. The combination options are editorially supplied because the source presents the candidate intervals as statements. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 16, 26 November 2020, page 8; answer key page 51.

items.topic: regression-t11 · conditional mean regression function with an indicator variable
items.stem: Suppose (X₁,Y₁),…,(Xₙ,Yₙ) are generated as follows: Y₁,…,Yₙ are i.i.d. Bernoulli(1/2), and Xᵢ conditional on Yᵢ=y has a Uniform(0,y+1) distribution. Define h(x)=1 if x≥1 and h(x)=0 otherwise. Which of the following is a correct linear regression model for m(x)=E(Yᵢ|Xᵢ=x), in the sense that the true m(x) is obtained for some values of α₀,α₁,α₂ for all x in the support?
items.explanation:
Use Bayes' rule to calculate the conditional probability that Y=1 after observing X=x. If Y=0, then X~Uniform(0,1), whose density is 1 on (0,1). If Y=1, then X~Uniform(0,2), whose density is 1/2 on (0,2). The prior probabilities of Y=0 and Y=1 are both 1/2.

For 0<x<1, both values of Y are possible. The joint density contributions are (1/2)×1 for Y=0 and (1/2)×(1/2) for Y=1. Therefore P(Y=1|X=x)=(1/4)/(1/2+1/4)=1/3.

For 1≤x<2, Y=0 is impossible because a Uniform(0,1) variable cannot exceed 1. Thus P(Y=1|X=x)=1. Since Y is binary, E(Y|X=x)=P(Y=1|X=x). Hence m(x)=1/3 for 0<x<1 and m(x)=1 for 1≤x<2. This can be written as m(x)=1/3+(2/3)h(x), which is option 4 with α₀=1/3, α₁=0 and α₂=2/3.

The supplied answer key on page 51 lists option 4. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 17, December 2019, page 8; answer key page 51.

items.topic: regression-t1 · diagonal leverage values in simple linear regression with an intercept
items.stem: Given data {(xᵢ,yᵢ): i=1,2,…,n}, where n≥2 and the xᵢ are not all identical, fit the simple linear regression model y=α+βx+ε. Let hᵢᵢ be the i-th diagonal element of the hat matrix H=X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ, where X is the n×2 model matrix. Which of the following are possible for some choice of n and x₁,…,xₙ?
statements: hᵢᵢ=−1 for some i.
hᵢᵢ=0 for some i.
hᵢᵢ=1 for some i.
All hᵢᵢ are equal.

A.why: A diagonal element of a projection matrix is a squared length, so it cannot be negative.

B.why: With an intercept and nonconstant x values, hᵢᵢ=1/n+(xᵢ−x̄)²/Σⱼ(xⱼ−x̄)², which is strictly positive.

C.why: For n=2 with two distinct x values, the 2×2 design matrix is square and full rank, so H=I and each leverage equals 1.

D.why: The same n=2 example has all diagonal leverages equal to 1.

items.explanation:
For simple linear regression with an intercept, the leverage of observation i is hᵢᵢ=1/n+(xᵢ−x̄)²/Sₓₓ, where Sₓₓ=Σⱼ(xⱼ−x̄)²>0.

This formula immediately rules out statement 1 because both terms are nonnegative. It also rules out statement 2 because the first term 1/n is strictly positive. Thus no observation can have leverage −1 or 0.

To show that statements 3 and 4 are possible, choose n=2 with x₁≠x₂. The design matrix X has two rows and two columns and is invertible. Therefore H=X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ=I₂. Its diagonal entries are h₁₁=h₂₂=1. So a leverage of 1 is possible and all leverages can be equal. Hence statements 3 and 4 only are correct.

**Printed-key discrepancy:** the supplied answer key on page 51 lists statements 2, 3 and 4. Statement 2 conflicts with the exact leverage formula: hᵢᵢ≥1/n>0. The bank records the mathematically supported answer (3 and 4) and preserves the source-key conflict. The combination options are editorially supplied because the scan lists statements but no combination choices. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 19, December 2019, page 9; answer key page 51.

items.topic: regression-t2 · pooled OLS slope and between-group covariance effects
items.stem: Two sets of observations on a random vector (X,Y) are available. In each set, a simple linear regression of Y on X with an intercept is fitted. Let β̂₁ and β̂₂ be the two within-set least-squares slopes, and let β̂₀ be the least-squares slope obtained by pooling the two sets. If β̂₁>β̂₂>0, which statement is true?
options: β̂₀ may lie outside (β̂₂,β̂₁), but it cannot exceed β̂₁+β̂₂.
β̂₀ may lie outside (β̂₂,β̂₁), but it cannot be negative.
items.explanation:
The pooled regression slope is not simply an average of the two within-set slopes. It also includes a between-set contribution caused by differences between the group means.

For two groups, the pooled numerator is the sum of the within-group cross-products plus a between-group term proportional to (x̄₁−x̄₂)(ȳ₁−ȳ₂). The pooled denominator is positive. If the group means move in opposite directions, the between-group numerator can be strongly negative even when both within-group slopes are positive.

For a concrete example, take three x values −1,0,1 in group 1 and y values 9,10,11, giving within-group slope 1. In group 2 take x values 9,10,11 and y values −11,−10,−9, again giving within-group slope 1. Both within-group slopes are positive, but the groups have very different means in opposite directions. The pooled between-group cross-product is large and negative, so the pooled slope is negative. Thus statement D is true. The supplied answer key on page 51 lists D.

items.topic: regression-t2 · estimability of linear functions in a rank-deficient linear model
items.stem: Consider the linear model Yᵢ=θ₁+θ₂+εᵢ for i=1,2 and Yᵢ=θ₁−θ₃+εᵢ for i=3,4, where the errors are independent with mean zero and common variance σ²>0. Which of the following parametric functions is estimable?
items.explanation:
The model tells us that the first two observations have expectation θ₁+θ₂, while the last two have expectation θ₁−θ₃. Therefore the two combinations directly identified by the data are θ₁+θ₂ and θ₁−θ₃.

A linear combination is estimable if it can be written as a linear combination of these two identifiable mean combinations. Subtract the second from the first:

(θ₁+θ₂)−(θ₁−θ₃)=θ₂+θ₃.

This combination can be estimated by the difference between the two group sample means: (Ȳ₁+Ȳ₂)/2 − (Ȳ₃+Ȳ₄)/2. Hence θ₂+θ₃ is estimable, option C. The other listed functions cannot be formed from the two available mean combinations. The supplied answer key on page 51 lists option C.

Other-exam relevance: estimability, row spaces of design matrices and non-identifiable linear models are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t13 · exact and conservative confidence intervals from uniform order statistics
items.stem: Suppose X₁,…,Xₙ is a random sample from Uniform(θ,θ+1), where θ∈ℝ is unknown. Let X₍₁₎ and X₍ₙ₎ be the sample minimum and maximum. Which of the following are 100(1−α)% confidence intervals for θ (coverage at least 1−α)?

A.why: The coverage is exactly 1−α for statements 1 and 2. Statement 3 has coverage 1−2(α/2)^n, which is at least 1−α for n≥1.

B.why: Statement 2 has exact coverage 1−α.

C.why: Statement 3 is conservative but still has coverage at least 1−α; statement 4 is not a valid interval.

D.why: Statement 4 has coverage (1−α)^n, which is below 1−α for n>1.

items.explanation:
Write Uᵢ=Xᵢ−θ. Then U₁,…,Uₙ are i.i.d. Uniform(0,1). Let U₍₁₎ and U₍ₙ₎ be their minimum and maximum.

**Statement 1:** θ<X₍ₙ₎−α^(1/n) exactly when U₍ₙ₎>α^(1/n). Since P(U₍ₙ₎≤t)=tⁿ, the coverage is 1−(α^(1/n))ⁿ=1−α.

**Statement 2:** X₍₁₎+α^(1/n)−1<θ exactly when U₍₁₎<1−α^(1/n). Since P(U₍₁₎≥t)=(1−t)ⁿ, the coverage is 1−(α^(1/n))ⁿ=1−α.

**Statement 3:** The interval contains θ when U₍₁₎<1−α/2 and U₍ₙ₎>α/2. The two failure events (all Uᵢ≥1−α/2 and all Uᵢ≤α/2) are disjoint and each has probability (α/2)ⁿ. Thus coverage is 1−2(α/2)ⁿ, which is at least 1−α for n≥1. It is exact when n=1 and conservative for n>1.

**Statement 4:** Coverage is P(U₍₁₎>α)=(1−α)ⁿ, which is smaller than 1−α for n>1. So it is not a valid general 100(1−α)% interval. Statements 1, 2 and 3 only are valid under the usual at-least-nominal coverage definition.

**Printed-key discrepancy:** the supplied answer key on page 51 lists all four statements. Statement 4 does not achieve the stated coverage for n>1; the item preserves the key conflict and explains the probability calculation. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 26, December 2018, page 15; answer key page 51.

items.topic: regression-t2 · inference-t3 · full-rank linear models, BLUE and UMVU estimation
items.stem: Consider the three-observation linear model Y=Xβ+ε, where β=(β₁,β₂,β₃)ᵀ, X is a 3×3 matrix with nonzero determinant, and ε₁,ε₂,ε₃ are i.i.d. N(0,σ²). Let β̂ be the least-squares estimator of β and let ℓ₁,ℓ₂,ℓ₃ be arbitrary real constants. Which statements are true?
statements: The least-squares estimator β̂ is unique.
ℓ₁β̂₁+ℓ₂β̂₂+ℓ₃β̂₃ is the BLUE of ℓ₁β₁+ℓ₂β₂+ℓ₃β₃.
ℓ₁β̂₁+ℓ₂β̂₂+ℓ₃β̂₃ is the UMVU estimator of ℓ₁β₁+ℓ₂β₂+ℓ₃β₃.
ℓ₁β̂₁+ℓ₂β̂₂+ℓ₃β̂₃ is BLUE but not UMVU for the corresponding linear function.
items.explanation:
The nonzero determinant means X is invertible, so the three columns are linearly independent. The least-squares solution is therefore unique and equals β̂=X⁻¹Y. This proves statement 1.

Because the errors have mean zero and covariance matrix σ²I, β̂ is unbiased and has the smallest covariance matrix among all linear unbiased estimators. The Gauss–Markov theorem therefore gives the BLUE property for every linear combination ℓᵀβ. Statement 2 is true.

Under the stated normal model with full-rank square design, Y (equivalently β̂) contains the full sample information; the normal location-scale family is complete for the full mean vector and common variance. Thus the unbiased estimator ℓᵀβ̂ is also UMVU, so statement 3 is true. Statement 4 is false because it contradicts this UMVU property. The supplied answer key on page 51 lists statements 1, 2 and 3.

Other-exam relevance: full-rank linear models, Gauss–Markov BLUE and UMVU estimation under normality are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 27, June 2018, page 16; answer key page 51.

A.why: X is a square full-rank design matrix, so the least-squares solution is unique.

B.why: The Gauss–Markov theorem makes every linear contrast of the least-squares estimator BLUE.

C.why: Under the full-rank normal location-scale model, the complete sufficient statistic yields the UMVU estimator for every linear contrast.

D.why: The linear contrast is UMVU as well as BLUE, so it is not BLUE-but-not-UMVU.

items.topic: inference-t13 · shortest confidence intervals for a normal variance using a chi-square pivot
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. N(μ,σ²), where both μ and σ² are unknown. Consider the confidence interval Iₐ,ᵦ=[S/b,S/a] for σ², where S=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ(Xᵢ−X̄)² and b>a>0. Let Gₙ₋₁ be the CDF of a chi-square variable with n−1 degrees of freedom. Which statements are true?
statements: It is possible to choose a and b with ab=1 so that Iₐ,ᵦ has 95% confidence.
If Gₙ₋₁(a)=1−Gₙ₋₁(b)=0.025, then Iₐ,ᵦ is the shortest 95% confidence interval.
If Iₐ,ᵦ is the shortest 95% confidence interval in expected length, then a and b satisfy b−a=(n−3)log(b/a).
If Gₙ₋₁(b)−Gₙ₋₁(a)=0.95, then E[length(Iₐ,ᵦ)]=(n−1)(1/a−1/b)σ².

A.why: By continuity, a with b=1/a can be chosen so that the chi-square probability between a and b is 0.95.

B.why: Equal-tail probability allocation is not generally the shortest interval when minimising the expected length of S[1/b,1/a].

C.why: The expected-length optimum satisfies b−a=(n+1)log(b/a), not (n−3)log(b/a).

D.why: E(S)=(n−1)σ², so the expected interval length is (n−1)σ²(1/a−1/b).

items.explanation:
The pivotal quantity Q=S/σ² has a chi-square distribution with ν=n−1 degrees of freedom. Therefore Iₐ,ᵦ covers σ² exactly when a≤Q≤b, and its confidence coefficient is Gν(b)−Gν(a).

Statement 1 is true. Set b=1/a. As a increases continuously from 0 toward 1, Gν(1/a)−Gν(a) moves continuously from 1 toward 0. Hence some a gives coverage 0.95.

Statement 2 is false in general. Equal-tail endpoints allocate 0.025 to each tail, but the interval length on the σ² scale is S(1/a−1/b), not simply b−a. The shortest expected-length interval need not be equal-tailed.

For statement 3, minimise E[length]=E(S)(1/a−1/b)=(n−1)σ²(1/a−1/b), subject to Gν(b)−Gν(a)=0.95. The first-order condition is a²gν(a)=b²gν(b), where gν is the chi-square density. Substituting gν(t)∝t^(ν/2−1)e^(−t/2) gives b−a=(ν+2)log(b/a)=(n+1)log(b/a), not (n−3)log(b/a). Thus statement 3 is false as printed.

Statement 4 is true because E(S)=(n−1)σ². Therefore the expected length is (n−1)σ²(1/a−1/b).

**Printed-key discrepancy:** the supplied answer key on page 51 lists statements 1, 3 and 4. The source's condition in statement 3 is inconsistent with minimising the expected length of the displayed interval; the derived first-order condition has n+1, not n−3. The bank preserves the source wording and flags the discrepancy. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 28, June 2018, page 17; answer key page 51.

items.topic: regression-t2 · maximum-likelihood estimation and consistency in a normal location model with known trend
items.stem: Consider the regression model Yᵢ=α+βi+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, where εᵢ are independent N(0,1) random variables, α≠0 is unknown and β is known. If α̂ₙ is the maximum-likelihood estimator of α, which statement is true?
items.explanation:
Because β is known, subtract its contribution from each observation: Yᵢ−βi=α+εᵢ. These adjusted observations are independent normal variables with mean α and variance 1. The maximum-likelihood estimator of their common mean is their sample average, so α̂ₙ=(1/n)Σ(Yᵢ−βi)=Ȳ−β(n+1)/2.

Its expectation is E(α̂ₙ)=α, so it is unbiased for every n. Its variance is Var(α̂ₙ)=(1/n²)ΣVar(εᵢ)=n/n²=1/n. As n increases, 1/n tends to zero. Therefore option D is correct.

The condition α≠0 does not change this calculation; it simply rules out a special parameter value. The key idea is that a known trend can be removed before estimating the intercept.

Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 30, December 2017, page 19; printed answer key page 51 (D).

items.topic: inference-t13 · confidence intervals from the stability of the Cauchy distribution
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from the Cauchy distribution with density fθ(x)=1/{π[1+(x−θ)²]}, where θ∈ℝ is unknown. Which of the following proposed intervals have confidence coefficient 1−α for every 0<α<1?

A.why: A single Cauchy observation has the stated symmetric interval coverage, and the average of two independent standard-scale Cauchy observations is again Cauchy with the same location and scale.

B.why: The third proposed interval is not ordered for every α; for example, when 1−α is sufficiently large, its lower endpoint exceeds its upper endpoint.

C.why: The fourth proposed interval has the same endpoint-order problem for some confidence levels.

D.why: Statements 3 and 4 fail for part of the allowed range 0<α<1.

items.explanation:
A standard Cauchy variable Z has distribution function F(z)=1/2+(1/π)arctan(z). Therefore P(−c≤Z≤c)=2arctan(c)/π. If c=tan{π(1−α)/2}, then arctan(c)=π(1−α)/2 for 0<α<1, and the probability is exactly 1−α. This proves statement 1.

The Cauchy distribution is stable: if X₁ and X₂ are independent Cauchy(θ,1) variables, then (X₁+X₂)/2 is also Cauchy(θ,1). Thus the same symmetric interval around their average has coverage 1−α, proving statement 2.

For statements 3 and 4, the proposed lower and upper half-widths are not positive and correctly ordered throughout the full range 0<α<1. For example, when 1−α=0.8, tan{5π(1−α)/7}=tan(4π/7)<0, so the proposed lower endpoint is above the centre; its magnitude also makes it exceed the proposed upper endpoint. Hence these are not confidence intervals for every allowed α.

**Printed-key discrepancy:** the answer key on page 51 lists all four intervals. The endpoint-order check shows that statements 3 and 4 fail for some permitted confidence levels. The bank records statements 1 and 2 only and flags the discrepancy. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 31, December 2017, page 19; printed answer key page 51.

items.topic: regression-t2 · least-squares estimation with two exponential regressors
items.stem: Consider the regression model Yᵢ=β₁eⁱ+β₂e⁻ⁱ+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, where εᵢ are independent N(0,σ²) random variables. Let β̂₁ and β̂₂ be the ordinary least-squares estimators. Which statements are correct?
statements: E(β̂₁)=β₁.
E(β̂₂)=β₂.
Var(β̂₁)>Var(β̂₂).
Cov(β̂₁,β̂₂)<0.

A.why: The regression model is linear in its coefficients and has a full-rank design for n≥2 distinct index values; OLS is unbiased under zero-mean errors.

B.why: The same OLS unbiasedness result applies to the second coefficient.

C.why: Since S₁₁>S₂₂, Var(β̂₁)=σ²S₂₂/det is smaller than Var(β̂₂)=σ²S₁₁/det; the stated greater-than inequality is false.

D.why: The off-diagonal entry of the inverse of the 2×2 Gram matrix is negative because the two design columns have a positive inner product.

items.explanation:
Write the design matrix with first column x₁=(e,e²,…,eⁿ)ᵀ and second column x₂=(e⁻¹,e⁻²,…,e⁻ⁿ)ᵀ. The OLS estimator is β̂=(XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY. Since E(Y)=Xβ and E(ε)=0, E(β̂)=β. Thus statements 1 and 2 are true.

For two regressors, put S₁₁=x₁ᵀx₁, S₂₂=x₂ᵀx₂ and S₁₂=x₁ᵀx₂. The covariance matrix is σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹=σ²/(S₁₁S₂₂−S₁₂²) [[S₂₂,−S₁₂],[−S₁₂,S₁₁]]. Here S₁₂>0, so the covariance of the two coefficient estimates is negative. Also, for i≥1, e²ⁱ>e⁻²ⁱ, hence S₁₁>S₂₂. The variance of β̂₁ is proportional to S₂₂, while the variance of β̂₂ is proportional to S₁₁. Therefore Var(β̂₁)<Var(β̂₂), not greater.

**Important correction:** the printed key lists A, B and D. Statement C as printed says Var(β̂₁)>Var(β̂₂), but the inverse Gram-matrix formula gives the reverse inequality. Thus the mathematically correct statements are 1, 2 and 4 only (option C in the bank's combination list). Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 32, December 2017, page 20; printed answer key page 51 lists A, B, D.

items.topic: regression-t2 · nested least-squares models and residual sum-of-squares comparison
items.stem: For observations (xᵢ,yᵢ), fit Model 1: yᵢ=β₀+β₁xᵢ and Model 2: yᵢ=β₀+β₁xᵢ+β₂xᵢ² by least squares. Let A and B be the residual sums of squares from Models 1 and 2, respectively. Which statements are correct?
statements: A≥B.
A≤B.
It can happen that A=0 but B>0.
It can happen that B=0 but A>0.

A.why: Model 1 is contained in Model 2 by setting β₂=0. The larger model cannot have a larger minimum residual sum of squares.

B.why: The inequality is in the opposite direction; adding a predictor cannot increase the minimum least-squares residual sum of squares.

C.why: If Model 1 fits every observation exactly, Model 2 can reproduce that fit by taking β₂=0, so B must also be zero.

D.why: A quadratic model can fit data exactly even when no straight line does; for example, three points on a non-linear quadratic curve.

items.explanation:
Least squares chooses the coefficients that make the residual sum of squares as small as possible. Model 2 has every choice available to Model 1, because we can set its extra coefficient β₂=0. It also has additional choices with β₂≠0. Therefore the minimum residual sum of squares in Model 2 cannot exceed that in Model 1: B≤A. This proves statement 1 and disproves statement 2.

If A=0, the observations lie exactly on a straight line. Model 2 can use the same straight line by choosing β₂=0, so B=0 as well. Hence statement 3 is impossible. Conversely, a quadratic curve can pass exactly through the observations while no straight line does; then B=0 and A>0. Statement 4 is possible. Therefore statements 1 and 4 only are correct.

The supplied answer key on page 51 lists A and D, which agrees. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 36, June 2016, page 22; printed answer key page 51.

items.topic: inference-t13 · chi-square confidence interval for a normal variance with known mean
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from N(μ,σ²), where μ is known and σ²>0 is unknown. Let χ²ₙ,α/2 and χ²ₙ,1−α/2 denote the upper-tail α/2 and 1−α/2 quantiles of a chi-square distribution with n degrees of freedom. Which expression is a 100(1−α)% confidence interval for σ²?
items.explanation:
Because μ is known, each standardized squared deviation (Xᵢ−μ)²/σ² contributes to a chi-square pivot. In fact, Q=Σ(Xᵢ−μ)²/σ² has a chi-square distribution with n degrees of freedom. Notice the degrees of freedom are n, not n−1: we have not estimated μ from the sample.

Using the upper-tail quantile convention in the question, P(χ²ₙ,1−α/2≤Q≤χ²ₙ,α/2)=1−α. Replace Q by its expression and solve the two inequalities for σ². Since all quantities are positive, the lower endpoint uses the larger chi-square quantile and the upper endpoint uses the smaller one. This gives [Σ(Xᵢ−μ)²/(nχ²ₙ,α/2), Σ(Xᵢ−μ)²/(nχ²ₙ,1−α/2)] under the source's quantile notation: option D.

The other options either use the wrong centering, the wrong degrees of freedom, or the sample mean even though μ is known. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 38, June 2016, page 23; printed answer key page 51 (D).

items.topic: regression-t7 · projection matrices, leverage and residual variances in the linear model
items.stem: Consider Y=Xβ+ε, where X is n×p with rank p, E(ε)=0 and Var(ε)=σ²I. Let H=X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ=(hᵢⱼ) be the hat matrix. Which statements are correct?
statements: 0≤hᵢᵢ≤1 for every i.
If hᵢᵢ=0 or 1 for some i, then hᵢⱼ=0 for every j≠i.
Var(Ŷ)=σ²H, where Ŷ=HY.
Var(eᵢ)=σ²(1−hᵢᵢ), where eᵢ=Yᵢ−Ŷᵢ.

A.why: H is a symmetric idempotent projection matrix. Its diagonal elements are squared projection lengths and lie between zero and one.

B.why: For a projection matrix, Σⱼhᵢⱼ²=hᵢᵢ. If hᵢᵢ is 0 or 1, then hᵢᵢ−hᵢᵢ²=Σⱼ≠ᵢhᵢⱼ²=0, forcing every off-diagonal element in that row to be zero.

C.why: Ŷ=HY, so Var(Ŷ)=H(σ²I)Hᵀ=σ²H because H is symmetric and idempotent.

D.why: The residual vector is (I−H)Y, whose covariance matrix is σ²(I−H); its i-th diagonal element is σ²(1−hᵢᵢ).

items.explanation:
The hat matrix H=X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ is the matrix that projects the observed response vector Y onto the column space of X. It has two important properties: Hᵀ=H (symmetric) and H²=H (idempotent).

1. The diagonal hᵢᵢ is the leverage of observation i. Since H is a projection matrix, 0≤hᵢᵢ≤1.

2. From H²=H, the (i,i) entry gives Σⱼhᵢⱼ²=hᵢᵢ. Since H is symmetric, this becomes hᵢᵢ²+Σⱼ≠ᵢhᵢⱼ²=hᵢᵢ. Thus Σⱼ≠ᵢhᵢⱼ²=hᵢᵢ(1−hᵢᵢ). If hᵢᵢ=0 or 1, the sum of squares is zero, so all hᵢⱼ for j≠i are zero.

3. Since Ŷ=HY, Var(Ŷ)=H Var(Y)Hᵀ=σ²HHᵀ=σ²H.

4. The residual vector is e=(I−H)Y. Its covariance is σ²(I−H), so Var(eᵢ)=σ²(1−hᵢᵢ). All four statements are correct. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 41, June 2016, page 25; printed answer key page 51 (A, B, C, D).

items.topic: probability-t8 · compound geometric sums, moment-generating functions and characteristic functions
items.stem: Let N,A₁,A₂,… be independent, with P(N=k)=(1−p)pᵏ for k=0,1,2,…, where 0<p<1. Let A₁,A₂,… be i.i.d. bounded random variables and define X=0 when N=0 and X=Σⱼ₌₁ᴺAⱼ when N≥1. Which statements are necessarily correct?
statements: X is a bounded random variable.
M_X(t)=(1−p)/[1−pM_A(t)] for every real t.
φ_X(t)=(1−p)/[1−pφ_A(t)] for every real t.
X is symmetric about zero.

A.why: N has unbounded support. If Aᵢ=1 with probability one, then X=N, which is unbounded.

B.why: The geometric-series formula for the MGF is valid only where pM_A(t)<1; because N is unbounded, the MGF need not exist for every real t.

C.why: Conditioning on N gives φ_X(t)=Σₖ₌₀∞(1−p)pᵏφ_A(t)ᵏ, a convergent geometric series because |pφ_A(t)|≤p<1.

D.why: The summands need not be symmetric; for example, Aᵢ=1 almost surely makes X nonnegative.

items.explanation:
Condition on the value of N, the number of terms in the sum. If N=k, independence gives the characteristic function of A₁+⋯+Aₖ as [φ_A(t)]ᵏ. Therefore

φ_X(t)=Σₖ₌₀∞P(N=k)[φ_A(t)]ᵏ=(1−p)Σₖ₌₀∞[pφ_A(t)]ᵏ.

A characteristic function always has absolute value at most one. Hence |pφ_A(t)|≤p<1, so the geometric series converges for every real t and equals (1−p)/[1−pφ_A(t)]. Statement 3 is true.

The same formal calculation for the moment-generating function uses M_A(t) instead of φ_A(t), but it converges only when pM_A(t)<1. Boundedness of A does not guarantee this condition for every real t, because the number N of summands can be arbitrarily large. For example, if A=1 almost surely, then X=N and its MGF is finite only when peᵗ<1. Thus statement 2 is false as written.

Since N is unbounded, X need not be bounded; and since the summands need not be symmetric, X need not be symmetric. Statements 1 and 4 are false. Therefore statement 3 only is correct. The supplied scan's answer key on page 51 stops at Q41, so no printed key entry for Q49 is available in that key page; this answer is derived directly from the stated probability model. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 49, December 2015, page 30.

items.topic: inference-t7 · beta-binomial Bayesian estimation with the Jeffreys prior
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. Bernoulli(θ), 0<θ<1, and let S=ΣXᵢ. Suppose the prior density is proportional to [θ(1−θ)]⁻¹/². Which statements about the posterior mean of θ are correct?
statements: The posterior mean does not exist.
The posterior mean exists.
The posterior mean is larger than the MLE for every possible S.
The posterior mean is larger than the MLE for at least some possible values of S.

A.why: The posterior is a proper Beta distribution with positive shape parameters, so its mean exists.

B.why: The prior is Beta(1/2,1/2), so after observing S successes the posterior is Beta(S+1/2,n−S+1/2), which has a finite mean.

C.why: The posterior mean is not always above S/n; it is below the MLE when S>n/2.

D.why: For S<n/2, (S+1/2)/(n+1) exceeds S/n, so the posterior mean is larger for some possible values of S.

items.explanation:
The prior density proportional to 1/√[θ(1−θ)] is the Beta(1/2,1/2) prior. The likelihood from n Bernoulli observations is proportional to θˢ(1−θ)ⁿ⁻ˢ. Multiplying prior and likelihood gives a Beta(S+1/2,n−S+1/2) posterior.

The mean of a Beta(a,b) distribution is a/(a+b). Therefore the posterior mean is (S+1/2)/(n+1), which exists for every S=0,1,…,n. The MLE is S/n (including 0 and 1 at the two boundary samples).

Compare them: (S+1/2)/(n+1)−S/n=(n−2S)/[2n(n+1)]. This difference is positive when S<n/2, zero when S=n/2, and negative when S>n/2. So the posterior mean exists and is larger than the MLE for some, but not all, possible S values. Statements 2 and 4 only are correct. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 50, December 2014, page 31. The answer-key page supplied with this PDF ends at Q41, so no printed key entry for Q50 is visible.

items.topic: regression-t2 · estimable functions, row spaces and null spaces in linear models
items.stem: Consider the linear model E(Y)=Xβ and Cov(Y)=σ²I, where X is an n×p matrix of rank r≤p. Which statements are necessarily true?
statements: The set of estimable linear functions of β is a vector space of dimension r.
If E(cᵀY)=0 for some nonzero c, then at least one linear function of β is not estimable.
If every linear function ℓᵀβ is estimable, then r=p.
The set of vectors c for which E(cᵀY)=0 has dimension r.

A.why: Estimable coefficient vectors are exactly the row space of X, whose dimension is rank(X)=r.

B.why: E(cᵀY)=cᵀXβ=0 for all β implies Xᵀc=0. Since r≤p and c is nonzero, X cannot have full column rank p, so some coefficient function is not estimable.

C.why: All p-dimensional coefficient directions are estimable exactly when the row space of X is all of Rᵖ, which requires rank p.

D.why: The vectors c satisfying Xᵀc=0 form the null space of Xᵀ, whose dimension is n−r, not r.

items.explanation:
A linear function ℓᵀβ is estimable precisely when its coefficient vector ℓ belongs to the row space of X. The row space has dimension rank(X)=r, so statement 1 is true. Next, E(cᵀY)=cᵀXβ. For this expectation to be zero for every possible β, we need Xᵀc=0. Thus c is in the null space of Xᵀ. If a nonzero such c exists, the rank is less than n; more importantly, because rank(X)=r≤p and the existence of a nonzero c in the left null space alone does not imply r

p, statement 2 as printed needs careful interpretation. The supplied statement says there is a function ℓᵀβ which is not estimable. This follows only if rp. For example, a full-column-rank n×p matrix with n>p has nonzero left-null vectors but every coefficient function is estimable. Therefore statement 2 is NOT necessarily true. Statement 3 is true: all coefficient functions are estimable exactly when rank(X)=p. Statement 4 is false because dim Null(Xᵀ)=n−r. Hence the mathematically necessary statements are 1 and 3 only. The bank records the corrected answer and flags the logical flaw in statement 2. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 51, December 2014, page 31. items.topic: regression-t2 · estimability in a rank-deficient three-parameter linear model
items.stem: Consider the linear model with E(Y₁)=2θ+β, E(Y₂)=β+2γ and E(Y₃)=θ+β+γ, where θ, β and γ are unknown. Which of the following functions are estimable?
statements: θ, β and γ are all estimable.
θ−γ is estimable.
2γ−2θ is estimable.
θ+γ is estimable.

A.why: The design matrix has rank 2, so the three individual parameters cannot all be identified.

B.why: θ−γ is the linear combination one-half of E(Y₁) minus one-half of E(Y₂).

C.why: 2γ−2θ is −2(θ−γ), a scalar multiple of an estimable function.

D.why: θ+γ cannot be expressed as a linear combination of the three design rows.

items.explanation:
Write the design matrix as X=[[2,1,0],[0,1,2],[1,1,1]]. The third row is one-half the sum of the first two, so the matrix has rank 2, not 3. Therefore θ, β and γ cannot all be estimated separately. Statement 1 is false.

Now use the expectations: E(Y₁)=2θ+β and E(Y₂)=β+2γ. Their difference, divided by two, is [E(Y₁)−E(Y₂)]/2=θ−γ. Thus θ−γ is estimable, and any scalar multiple such as 2γ−2θ is also estimable.

But θ+γ cannot be formed from these identifiable combinations. To see this, any row-space vector has form a(2,1,0)+b(0,1,2)=(2a,a+b,2b). Setting this equal to (1,0,1) would require a=b=1/2 but then the middle coordinate is 1, not 0. So θ+γ is not estimable. Statements 2 and 3 only are correct. Source: Methods of Estimation PDF, Question 52, December 2014, page 32. The supplied answer-key page does not include Q52.
